text: (r) Καθὸ Θεός ἐστιν. Pugnat responsio hæc cum Chrys. hom. 35 in Joan. et Cyrill. Hi enim putant, judiciaria hac universa potestate, Christi deitatem maxime astrui; quam a Patre dicatur accepisse, uti et vitam, ipsa generatione; ut sicut vivus Filius, sic et Judex natus intelligatur; qui proinde, ut judex, ex his verbis Judæos percellat; idcirco nimirum, quod, ut ait idem Chrys., Εὐεργετούμενοι ἄνθρωποι οὐχ οὕτω προσάγονται, ὡς τιμωρούμενοι: Non sic beneficiis adducuntur ac suppliciis. Ubi interpr., Beneficia accepta non ita sentiunt; quomodo Cat. auctor sibi composuit, εὐεργετούμενοι οὐχ οὕτως αἰσθάνονται. Sed debuit alteram partem comparationis addere, ὡς τιμωρούμενοι, quam et interpr. Chrys. male omisit. Tantam vero Chrys. Filii cum Patre æqualitatem his importari existimavit, ut Sabellianæ objectioni occurrendum putaverit, et ne ipse Filius, qui Pater, crederetur: Οὐκοῦν καὶ Πατέρα αὐτὸν προσεροῦμεν; Ἄπαγε. Διὰ γὰρ τοῦτο εἶπεν τὸν Υἱόν, ἵνα μένοντα Υἱὸν, τιμῶμεν ὡς τὸν Πατέρα· Num ergo et Patrem nuncupabimus? Absit! Id enim causæ est cur Filium dixerat, ut cum Filius maneat, honoremus eum sicut Patrem. Ubi inscite interpr. Igitur Patrem præponemus? Sunt hæc quidem bona, non tamen Maximi quæstionem expediunt: cur Filius, non Pater judicaturus dicatur. Uterque enim judicabit in ea sententia: Pater, ut auctor; Filius, ut qui habeat a Patre. Maximus ad judicium refert comparationis, ut vita sua Christus, nostram judicaturus sit; quomodo plerique apostolos judices cum Christo futuros interpretantur; longeque potiori ratione reginam Austri et Ninivitas. Sicque liquet, nec Deum proprie judicare homines, nec homines bruta; quod alius sit Dei modus, alius hominis; aliusque hominis, et brutarum animantium alius. Verum hic modus nihil singulare Christo tribuit, proque illius majestate. Melius itaque August. tract. 22 in Joan. de judicio manifesto exponit; in eadem ipsa forma, qua ascendit; in forma scilicet servi: in qua et vere accepit a Patre, uti exponit Hier. Matth. xxviii: Data est mihi omnis potestas, etc., et in qua omnes Filium honorare debent, sicut honorant et Patrem, quod idem vere Dei Filius est et Deus, qui filius hominis, et cui nihil ex assumpta forma servi decesserit.
anchorLine: Καθὸ Θεός ἐστιν (r), οὐδὲ ὁ Πατήρ, οὐδὲ ὁ Υἱὸς
en: This answer clashes with Chrysostom (Hom. 35 on John) and Cyril. They hold that by this whole judicial power Christ's deity is chiefly established, since he is said to have received it from the Father, as he received life, by generation: as the Son is living, so he is understood to be born Judge, and so, as judge, he strikes the Jews with these words. This is, as Chrysostom says, because men who receive benefits are not drawn as those who are punished are: 'They are not drawn so by benefits as by punishments.' The translator renders this 'Benefits received are not so felt'; the Catena author wrote for himself 'those who receive benefits do not feel it so'. But he should have added the other half of the comparison, 'as those being punished', which Chrysostom's translator also wrongly left out. Chrysostom thought such equality of Son with Father was implied here that he felt bound to meet the Sabellian objection, lest the Son himself be taken for the Father: 'Shall we then call him Father too? Far from it. He said Son so that, while he remains Son, we honour him as the Father.' The translator wrongly renders 'Shall we then put the Father first?' These points are good, but they do not settle Maximus's question, why the Son and not the Father is said to be going to judge. Both will judge in that sense: the Father as author, the Son as one who has it from the Father. Maximus refers the judgment to a comparison: Christ will judge our life by his own, as most take the apostles to be future judges with Christ, and far more fittingly the queen of the South and the Ninevites. So it is plain that God does not judge men in the proper sense, nor men beasts, since God's way is one, man's another, and man's differs again from that of beasts. But this way gives Christ nothing singular, nothing proper to his majesty. Augustine (Tract. 22 on John) therefore explains the judgment better, as manifest, in the very form in which he ascended, that is the form of a servant, in which he truly received from the Father, as Jerome explains on Matt. 28, 'All power is given to me', and in which all must honour the Son as they honour the Father, since the same is truly Son of God and God, who is Son of man, and loses nothing from the form of a servant he assumed.

text: (s) Φασὶ τινες. Quod hic Maximus tantis vexat, de modis quibus peccata, etiam nobis non pœnitentibus, indulgeantur, refertque tanquam ex veterum sententia, aliquid difficultatis habet, nisi dicamus (quod et ipse non obscure habet) sermonem esse de oblitis, quæ memoria assequi non possumus; quorum proinde non potest esse expressus dolor, sed solum implicitus, ac virtualis pœnitentia, quam ipsam velut impetrent, proximorum miseratio, et quod alios minime judicemus; vel etiam alii aliorum delicta ignoscamus. Sic et passim Chrys. salutis parandæ vias veniæque exaggerat: quæ omnia sic ἀνθρωπινώτερον dicta, modo jam dicto exponenda sunt, non velut quis, graviorum scelerum reus, absque interiori in hac vita pœnitentia, saltem virtuali, veraque charitate, veniam aut regnum consequatur. Qua de re jam annot. n. 8. Ad ærumnas ac necessitates quod attinet, purgant hæ quidem; sed qui ferat patienter, Deumque in eis ultorem agnoscat ac colat; sin vero, reatum augent; nec video quæ purgatio, cum inter vitæ mala quis in Deum ingratus est ac morosus. De loco hic vexato, plura ex Patribus in Bibl. PP. concionat.
anchorLine: τέον. Φασὶ τινὲς (s) τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα διὰ τοῦ Πνεύμα-
en: What Maximus presses so hard here, the ways sins are forgiven even to those who do not repent, which he reports as from the old opinion, is somewhat difficult, unless we say (as he plainly says himself) that it concerns forgotten sins, which memory cannot reach; for these there can be no express sorrow, only implicit or virtual repentance, which neighbours' mercy and our not judging others, or forgiving others' faults, win for them. Chrysostom likewise urges the ways of preparing salvation and pardon throughout; all this, said in a rather human manner, is to be read as just stated, not as if a man guilty of grave crimes could gain pardon or the kingdom without inward repentance in this life, at least virtual, and true charity. On this see annotation 8 already. As for hardships and necessities, they do purge, but only for one who bears them patiently and recognises and worships God as avenger in them; otherwise they add to guilt; and I see no purgation for one ungrateful and sullen toward God amid life's evils. On this troubled passage, the Bibl. PP. gather more from the Fathers.

text: (t) Ἐχθρὸν ἔχομεν. Paulo remotior videtur hæc allegoria. Clara littera, quam prosequuntur Isid. lib. iv, epist. 11, et Theodor. Rom. xii. Est vero adhortatio ad ferendas fortiter injurias, et iis, qui inferunt, contrariis rependendum, præbendaque illis necessaria: quæ videlicet, philosophantibus coronas contexant, pœnam vero injuriarum auctoribus augeant. Monet tamen Theodoret. non eo animo præstanda hæc hortari Apostolum, quod ad virtutem inducat ac philosophiam: sic tamen Salomoni scriptum admittit Isidor. nec eo documento magnum aliquid ac eximium contineri, sed quod etiam optandum; in eas angustias videre redactum inimicum, ut (quod illi omni gravius supplicio) a te cibum potumque exspectare debeat. Quod eo munere charitatis ardoribus inimici mens succendenda sit, atque ad meliora transferendus animus (in quo ipso Maximi allegoria est) non probat Isid. Τοῖς γὰρ λέγουσιν, ὅτι θερμανεῖς αὐτοῦ τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ ἀνανῆψαι ποιήσεις, οὐ πάνυ προσεκτέον. Chrys. hom. 22 in Epist. ad Rom. ex qua sua mutuatus, ut solet, Isidor. rite exponit Apostoli mentem, terrentis gravissimæ pœnæ metu, qui injuriam faciat, eumque qui sit passus hortantis ut inimico sufficiat sic dejecto, ut in vitæ necessariis illo egeat: quod præstando, ad ejus tandem dilectionem proficiat; etsi forte primum, exulceratum injuria animum, ea ipsa præstatione pœnaque inimici recreabat.
anchorLine: Ἐχθρὸν ἔχομεν (t) κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς, τὸ ἡμέτερον
en: This allegory seems rather remote. The plain letter is what Isidore (bk 4, ep. 11) and Theodoret on Rom. 12 follow: an exhortation to bear injuries bravely, to repay those who inflict them with the opposite, and to give them what they need, which weaves crowns for those who practise philosophy and heaps punishment on the wrongdoers. Theodoret warns, however, that the Apostle does not urge this as leading to virtue and philosophy; Isidore grants this was written to Solomon, but says no great or choice teaching is contained in it, only something to be wished: that the enemy be brought to such straits that he must look to you for food and drink, which is worse for him than any punishment. Isidore does not approve the idea that the enemy's mind is to be fired with the burning coals of charity and his spirit turned to better things (which is Maximus's own allegory): 'one should not much heed those who say you will warm his ruling part and make him revive.' Isidore, borrowing from Chrysostom (Hom. 22 on Romans) as usual, rightly gives the Apostle's meaning: he warns the wrongdoer with fear of the gravest punishment, and urges the injured to supply the enemy so cast down that he lacks life's necessities, so that by giving he may at last win his love, though perhaps at first the injured spirit was soothed by that very giving and the enemy's punishment.

text: (u) Ὁ πελεκὰν οὗτος. Quod hic de pelicano refert Maximus, ejusque in pullos amore, eorumque suscitatione, ex vulgi usu petitum, ac fabulosum est; etsi ita censuerunt nonnulli Patrum, Epiph. in Physiol., Eustath. in Hexaem., August. psal. ci, Greg., Isid., Orig. l. xii, c. 7, qui tamen, non ut Maximus, ejus pullos a serpente necari tradunt, sed ab ipsis parentibus nimiis osculis; alii a masculo, alii a femella. Imposuit viris sanctis, qui primus hanc fabellam mendacio suo adornavit; quam illi proclive arripuere, quasi faventem mysterio resurrectionis: quod tamen supra naturæ vires exsistens, aliunde sua momenta petit. Non videtur esse eadem avis, quæ psal. ci, 8; Levit. xi, 18, קאת, pelicanus dicitur, sic dicta a vomitu, quod conchas gurgulione exceptas inque illo calefactas evomat, ipsa nimirum platea, et quæ grammaticis Græcis Hesych., Suid., aliisque describitur, Πελεκᾶς ὄρνεον τὸ κολάπτον καὶ τρυπῶν τὰ δένδρα, ἀφ' οὗ καὶ δενδροκολάπτης· Avis tundens arbores easque perforans, unde et nomen habet: nempe picus martius. Nihil sane utrique avi commune. Avem sic in pullos amore proclivem, non quæ suo cruore exstinctos suscitet, sed quæ illo mortis periculum ab inedia arceat, vere φιλόστοργος, quod ipsa vox Hebraica sonat רחם, quasi misericors, vulturem ostendit Bochart. Arias vocem φιλόστοργος posuit, quod non est rem explicare, sed vocis etymum dare; quod in Aquila quandoque carpit Hier. Vulg. illo Levit. ii cygnum habet. Alii exponunt meropem; aitque Buxt. sic dictam avem ab amore et misericordia erga parentes, quod eos in altissimis rupibus reconditos alat, ut auctor est Plin. l. x, c. 53. At vox Hebr. potius φιλότεχνον significat. Vultur
anchorLine: Ὁ πελεκὰν οὗτος (u) ὀρνεόν ἐστιν· ὁ δὲ ὄφις, πολὺ
en: What Maximus says of the pelican, its love for its young and their revival, comes from popular belief and is fable, though some Fathers (Epiphanius, Eustathius, Augustine, Gregory, Isidore, Origen) held it; they say the young are killed not by a serpent but by the parents' over-fond kisses, or by the male or the female. Whoever first dressed up this tale with his lie imposed on holy men, who took it up readily as favouring the mystery of the resurrection, which however stands above nature and draws its force elsewhere. The bird of Ps. 101:8 and Lev. 11:18 (Hebrew qa'at, rendered pelican) seems not the same: it is the platea, which vomits shells it has swallowed and warmed in its gullet, and the Greek lexicographers describe the pelekas as the bird that strikes and pierces trees, the woodpecker, which has nothing in common with the pelican. Bochart shows that the bird loving its young, as the Hebrew word rachem suggests, 'merciful', is the vulture. Arias gave the word philostorgos, which explains the word's etymology, not the thing; Jerome sometimes criticises this in Aquila; the Vulgate has 'swan' in Lev. 11. Others say bee-eater; Buxtorf says the bird is named for love and mercy toward its parents, since it feeds them hidden high in the rocks, as Pliny reports (bk 10, ch. 53). But the Hebrew word rather means philotechnon, fond of offspring. Vulture

text: avis omnium minime noxia. Plutarch. in Romulo et in Romanis quæst. δικαιότατον καὶ ἀβλαβέστατον probat triplici ratione, quod nihil vivum attingat, sed solum morticinis utatur; quod a sui generis etiam morticinis abstineat; quod segetes humanosque labores nihil lædat. Horus Apollo l. i, c. 11, auctor est, Ægyptios in hieroglyphicis suis, misericordem picto vulture significasse. Μητέρα δὲ γράφοντες ἢ ἐλεήμονα, γῦπα ζωγραφοῦσι: Ut matrem aut misericordem significent, vulturem pingunt. Sed et senes jamque deplumes a pullis ali in monte Atlante tradit Scaliger in Card. exercit. 231, hincque scite aliud verbum jam Græcis fingendum ait, quam ἀντιπελαργεῖν (nempe ἀντοιωνεῖν) ad gratitudinis illam vicem pullorum in parentes significandam, sic olim in ciconiis celebratam, et quæ eadem in vulturibus eluceat. Nam οἰωνός, ὄρνις ὁ γύψ. Etymol. mag. Varin et alii passim. Nec quod ita dictum sit ac lusum, debuit male habere virum doctum, quasi Græcorum id convicio, aut non satis Græce dictum.
en: The vulture is the least harmful of birds; Plutarch (Romulus; Roman Questions) calls it most just and harmless for three reasons: it touches nothing living and uses only carrion, it keeps even from the carrion of its own kind, and it does no harm to crops or human labours. Horapollo says the Egyptians in their hieroglyphs signified a merciful one by a vulture, painting a vulture for 'mother' or 'merciful'. Scaliger reports that old and bald parents are fed by their young on Mount Atlas, and says Greeks should coin a new word, antipelargein (antoionein), for this return of kindness by the young to parents, once ascribed to storks and shining in vultures too. A learned man need not take it ill that this was said in play, as if it were a taunt on the Greeks or poor Greek.

text: (v) Ἐκεῖ στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσουσι. Nempe in cedris Libani: quod proinde de avibus communiter accipi debet, non de passeribus, quos liquet non nidificare in altis adeo montibus, sicque excelsis arboribus. Unde Aquil. Ἐκεῖ ὄρνεα νοσσεύσουσι.. Et Hieronymus: Ibi aves nidificabunt. Quod hic Maximus, ἢ τὰς διαφόρους ἀρετὰς exponit, valde tropologicum est: aptius ad allegoriam, quod in simili Hieronymus, Matth. xiii, volucres cœli dicit, vel animas credentium, vel fortitudines Dei servitio mancipatas: quas scilicet Δυνάμεις Græci proclive vocant: ἀρετὰς vero nunquam.
anchorLine: Τί ἐστιν, « Ἐκεῖ στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσουσι (v) ; »
en: That is, in the cedars of Lebanon, so it should be taken of birds generally, not of sparrows, which plainly do not nest on such high mountains and lofty trees. Hence Aquila has 'birds' and Jerome 'there birds will nest'. Maximus's reading of them as the various virtues is very tropological; more fitting to allegory is Jerome on Matt. 13, who takes the birds of heaven as the souls of believers or the powers of God given to his service, which Greeks readily call powers, never virtues.

text: (x) Ἐρωδιοῦ ἡ κατοικία ἡγεῖται αὐτῶν. Ἐρωδιόν, alii fulicam, alii ciconiam interpretantur; quæ sic in sublimibus nidulatur; crebrius quidem in turribus, quandoque etiam in arboribus. Velit textus Græcus, supra aves alias altius nidulari: hoc enim volucrum κατοικία. Hebr. habent ברושים, abietes domus ejus, quo significatur in abietibus, quæ sint procerae arbores, altisque insideant montibus, perinde ac cedri, nidificare. LXX et Hieron. quod sic reddiderunt, legerunt בראשים, in capitibus, in verticibus, qui est optimus sensus, eoque magis consentaneus, quod de excelsis omnibus, in quibus nidulatur ciconia, possit accipi, quæ sunt crebrius; non proceræ abietes, sed turrium celsarumque ædium fastigia. Sunt qui ardeam velint: eique convenit, quod hic Maximus in typum accipit castitatis, quod copulatam coitumque non appetit; Nempe quia sine dolore non coit. Philosoph. l. ix, c. 1: Τῶν δὲ ἐρωδιῶν ἐστι τρία γένη· ὅ τε πέλλος καὶ ὁ λευκός, καὶ ὁ ἀστερίας καλούμενος. Τούτων ὁ πέλλος χαλεπῶς εὐνάζει τε καὶ ὀχεύει· κράζει τε γάρ, καὶ αἷμα, ὥς φασιν, ἀφίησιν ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὀχεύων. Unde Plin. l. x, c. 60: Ardeolarum tria genera, leucon, asterias, pellus. Hi in coitu anguntur. Mares quidem cum vociferatu, sanguinem ex oculis profundunt. Hincque Etymolog. et Eustat. Ἰλιάδ. κ. nomen deducunt, παρὰ τὸ ἔαρ vel ἔωρ, id est, sanguine, et ἰδρύειν, quod est, sudare. Alii forte melius, ἐρωδιὸν volunt, quasi ἑλωδιὸν; id est, palustrem, quod locis palustribus delectetur.
markerNote: first Hebrew word read at 3x zoom as ברושים; letter-forms slightly ambiguous
anchorLine: Τί σημαίνει τὸ, « Ἐρωδιοῦ ἡ κατοικία ἡγεῖται αὐτῶν (x) ; »
en: Erodion is taken by some as the coot, by others as the stork, which nests high, more often on towers, sometimes in trees. The Greek text means it nests higher than other birds, since katoikia is the birds' dwelling. The Hebrew has 'firs', which would mean nesting in tall firs on high mountains like the cedars. The Septuagint and Jerome read 'in heads', 'on tops', the best sense, suited to the stork's nesting on towers and high roofs, not tall firs. Others say the heron, which fits Maximus's taking it as a type of chastity, since it avoids mating, because it does not mate without pain. The Philosopher (bk 9, ch. 1) names three kinds of heron and says the pellos mates with difficulty, crying and, as they say, shedding blood from the eyes; so Pliny (10.60). From this Etymologicum and Eustathius derive the name from 'blood' and 'to sweat'. Others, better perhaps, read 'marsh bird', since it delights in marshy places.

text: (y) Πρώτην γενεάν. Maximi hæc doctrina, quod suggestio, primaque velut apprehensio, ac qui eam sequitur, animi concupiscentis motus, ante consensum ac deliberatam rationem, seu etiam actionem, quæ sit vere actus humanus, seu hominis agentis ex consilio nutuque rationis et ut liber est, a Deo non puniantur, nondum in eis completa ratione peccati, sed quadam illius inchoatione, cujus ipsa compressio virtutis laude non careat, vera morum doctrina est: remotior tamen tropologia videtur ex illo Deut. loco, cujus mitior fere Græcorum expositio est. Peccantibus prima, secunda, tertia et quarta generationibus Deoque differente pœnam pro sua clementia, quartam tandem generationem puniri velut esset omnium rea; quasi in ea completa peccatorum mensura, ultra quam Dei decreto non erat proroganda illius clementia. Quod liquido ita contigisse videmus in veteri populo; Deo sæpius indulgente; tumque, obstinata eorum malitia, pœnam immittente: nec alio spectat sequens post alteram quæstio, de tribus et quatuor sceleribus Tyri et aliorum.
anchorLine: Πρώτην γενεὰν (z) ὑπειλήφαμεν εἶναι, τὴν σπο-
markerNote: the call in the Greek text prints as a letter that looks like z (flat, no descender) while the note is headed (y); both recorded as printed
en: Maximus's teaching is that the suggestion, the first apprehension, and the stirring of desire that follows it, before consent and deliberate reason or even action (which is truly a human act, a person acting by counsel and consent of reason as a free being), are not punished by God, since the full character of sin is not yet in them, only a beginning of it, and restraining that earns praise: this is true moral teaching. The tropology looks rather remote from that passage of Deuteronomy, which the Greeks mostly explain more mildly: for sinners in the first, second, third and fourth generations, with God differing his punishment out of clemency, the fourth generation is finally punished as if guilty of all, as though the measure of sins were complete and God's decree allowed his mercy no further delay. We see this happening in the old people, God often forgiving and then, their malice obstinate, sending punishment; and the next question, on the three and four crimes of Tyre and others, has the same bearing.

text: (a) Οὐκ ἀποστραφήσομαι. Addunt οἱ LXX αὐτήν. Sixt. interpr. Non aversabor eam. Quod sane abhorret: melius Vulg. Non convertam eam; quod Hebraica vox omnino significat, לא אשיבנו, ipsaque Græca nulla vi exponi potest: utrumque enim, et si contraria, significat τὸ, ἀποστρέφομαι, pro subjecta materia; exstantque passim in Lexicogr. exempla: nec in eo pœna est, quam Deus comminatur, quod non aversetur sceleratas civitates ac populos, sed quod non convertat.
anchorLine: δσεβείαις Τύρου οὐκ ἀποστραφήσομαι (a) ; »
en: The Septuagint adds 'it'. Sixtus's translator has 'I will not turn away from it', which is repugnant; the Vulgate 'I will not convert it' is better, as the Hebrew word plainly means, and the Greek cannot be explained otherwise: the verb means both senses, which are opposed, according to the matter at hand, as the lexica show. The punishment God threatens is not that he will not turn away from wicked cities and peoples, but that he will not convert them.

text: (b) Διὰ μέσου δὲ τοῦ Λόγου. Hæc vera processionis Spiritus doctrina, vera confessio, verbis solum a Latinorum de ea confessione diversa: quod Latini, utrumque, Patrem scilicet et Filium, ejus αἴτιον esse dicant, id est, auctorem, exque illis ut uno principio, seu auctore, procedere; Patre scilicet ipso totius deitatis fonte, qui tamen sic Filium ac Verbum ipse unus gignat, ut per Filium velut os suum, unumque cum eo principium unus Spirator Spiritum profundat: non ea solum ratione qua eo creaturas impartit, quæ frigida schismate laborantis, sequioris Græciæ commentitiaque solutio est, sed qua vere emanat, vera in Deitate persona; cujus ipsius emanationis modum a Filio perinde ac a Patre explicat, quod sic a Patre et Filio promiscue dari dicitur, et amborum Spiritus esse, ac sicut Filius παρὰ τοῦ Πατρὸς, a Patre Spiritum Veritatis, id est suum, ut Cyrillus interpretatur, habet, sic et παρὰ τοῦ Πατρὸς habet, ut ipsum cum Patre (principium scilicet ex principio unumque ipse cum eo principium) produceat. Optaram omnino ut Leo Allatius, tertium suum tomum Græciæ orthodoxæ produceret, ne accepti a me Georgii Metochitæ libri, quibus ille catholicam fidem strenue propugnat, exque traditione, mihi perirent, nec in communem, cui destinatum, utilitatem cederent. Ac vero periere ejus morte, quisquis sibi usurpaverit.
anchorLine: τοῦ Πνεύματος, διὰ μέσου δὲ τοῦ Λόγου (b). Καὶ
en: This is the true doctrine of the procession of the Spirit, a true confession differing from the Latins' only in words: the Latins say both Father and Son are its cause, that is, author, and that it proceeds from them as from one principle; the Father himself being the source of the whole deity, who yet begets the Son and Word alone in such a way that, through the Son as his mouth, and one principle with him, one Spirator pours out the Spirit; not only in the sense that he imparts it to creatures, which is the cold, schism-ridden, contrived solution of the lesser Greece, but as truly proceeding, a true person in the Deity. Maximus explains the manner of this emanation from the Son as from the Father, since the Spirit is said to be given by Father and Son together and to be the Spirit of both; as the Son has the Spirit of Truth, that is his own, from the Father, as Cyril interprets, so he also has it from the Father so as to produce it with the Father (a principle from a principle, one principle with him). The editor had hoped Leo Allatius would publish his third volume of Graecia Orthodoxa, so that the books of George Metochites defending the Catholic faith, which were received from him, would not be lost and would serve the common good for which they were meant. They have however perished with his death, whoever has appropriated them.

text: (c) Ἐπήρθη ὁ ἥλιος. Sic Græca et Cyril, a quibus non abludit Maximi tropologia: Hebr. tamen, Chald. Syr. Vulg. nec non Theodoret. prioribus jungunt, ut sit, Τὸ ὕψος τῆς φαντασίας αὐτῆς ἐπήρθη: ac tunc, sequatur, ὁ ἥλιος κ. τ. ἑ. Cyril. αὐτῆς, id est, ἀβύσσου: altitudo τῆς ἐν αὐτῇ φαντασίας, τουτέστιν, inquit, πᾶν ὅσον ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτῇ (credentium scilicet multitudine, uti ipse exponit) λαμπρόν τε καὶ ἐπηρμένον, καὶ ταῖς ἐν τῷδε τῷ κόσμῳ φαντασίαις, ἤτοι δόξαις κεναῖς κατηγλαϊσμένον, ἔδωκε φωνὴν αὐτῆς: ejus quæ in ipsa magnificentia est et splendor (nempe quidquid in ea splendidum est et excelsum, mundique hujus pompatico cultu; inani scilicet claritate magnifice ornatum) dedit vocem suam. Eodem sensu usurpata hæc vox Lucæ Act. xxv: Τῇ οὖν ἐπαύριον, ἐλθόντος τοῦ Ἀγρίππα καὶ τῆς Βερνίκης μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας. Vulg. cum multa ambitione: cum magno scilicet fastu et ostentatione seu apparatu (quod reddit Erasm.) atque ornatu: magnifico cultu ac comitatu. Suid. incerto auctore, Αὖθις δὲ Ῥωμαῖοι μετὰ μεγάλης φαντασίας καὶ συμπαθείας τοῦ δήμου προῆγον, Magno apparatu ac pompa. Usus est et Athen. aliique; longeque a vero abest Nobil. qui Cyrillum et Theodoret. abyssi cogitationem interpretatos dicat. Cyril. quid velit, cæcus est qui non videat: Theodoret., qua brevitate utitur, rem levius perstringit, nec eam vocem pluribus explicat. Major proinde fides, nedum ἀκρίβεια mihi in Nobilio desideretur. Vocem [...], id est, manus suas sic metaphorice οἱ LXX reddere potuerunt; uti etiam alii robur, amplitudinem, aliaque in illis reddunt.
anchorLine: Τί δηλοῖ τὸ, « Ἐπήρθη ὁ ἥλιος (c), καὶ ἡ
unreadable_part: the Hebrew word after 'Vocem' is not reliably legible (restored as [...])
en: So the Greek and Cyril read, and Maximus's tropology does not depart from them; but the Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac, Vulgate and Theodoret join the words to the preceding, so that it runs 'the height of its vision was lifted up', and then follows 'the sun...'. Cyril takes 'its' as of the abyss: the height of the vision in it, that is, all that is in it (the multitude of believers, as he explains), bright and lifted up, adorned with the show and empty glories of this world, gave its voice: that is, of the magnificence and splendour in it (whatever is brilliant and lofty in it, magnificently adorned with this world's pomp and empty brightness) gave its voice. Luke uses the same word in the same sense in Acts 25: 'when Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp'; the Vulgate has 'with much ambition', that is, with great show and display, which Erasmus renders. Suidas, from an unknown author, uses it too, and Athenaeus and others; Nobilius is far from the truth in saying Cyril and Theodoret took it as 'thought of the abyss'. What Cyril means, only a blind man would miss; Theodoret passes over it lightly in his brevity and does not explain the word further. I should thus have wanted more trust, let alone accuracy, in Nobilius. The Hebrew word for 'its hands' the Septuagint could render metaphorically; others render 'strength' and 'breadth' and the like.

text: (d) Περὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ κατακλυσμῷ. Locus hic difficilior est. Exponit Maximus, ut et scholia Græca, de mortuis ante Christum, non satis illius imbutis fide: nec desunt ex scholasticis, qui eam fidem Christi explicatam ad ingressum regni necessariam putarent, quam Christus descensu suo ad inferos Patribus invexerit. Sicque forsitan Maximus et scholia possint intelligi, de illis qui vel sanctis moribus vitam traduxissent, vel de malis commissis pœnituissent, cum explicatior illa Christi fides illis desideraretur; non qui graviorum scelerum rei, vivis excessissent: de illis denique, quos illatæ divinitus pœnæ ad saniorem mentem reduxissent; quales erant, quos diluvii aquæ sustulissent. Par sane est, plurimos qui Noemo fabricanti arcam præ incredulitate illuserant, aquis paulatim crescentibus, cunctisque commune exitium afferentibus, divinam justitiam cogitasse, eamque placare studuisse, serio pœnitendo, ipsumque, quoad ita delebantur, scelerum suorum ἀπόλυτρον, illisque expiandis probo animo a Deo suscepisse: quomodo passim etiam scelestissimos videmus in ipso patibulo omni patientia tormenta sustinere, Deoque offerre, hoc exorantes, ut iis misericordiam ab eo consequantur; quibus nec deest latronis exemplum, cui sic propense Christus indulsit in cruce, quod vel in extremis suorum scelerum, ejusque cum majestatis tum innocentiæ confessor, cultorque exstitisset. Grot. de fidelibus exponit, et quibus esset prædicata Christi fides, sed jam mortui essent, κατὰ ἀνθρώπου; carne, hominum existimatione, vel etiam eorum dolo et machinatione, qui solam carnem et corpus possunt occidere; viverent vero spiritu secundum Deum, ea vita cujus Deus auctor est: animi scilicet ac spiritali, uti Stephanus et Jacobus, qui jam sublati hominibus, Deo viverent.
anchorLine: Ἐπειδὴ περὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ κατακλυσμῷ (d) εἴρηται
en: This is a rather difficult passage. Maximus, like the Greek scholia, explains it of those dead before Christ, not well imbued with faith in him; and some scholastics held that explicit faith in Christ was necessary for entering the kingdom, a faith Christ brought to the Fathers by his descent to the underworld. So Maximus and the scholia may perhaps be understood of those who had either lived holy lives or repented of evils done, but lacked the fuller faith in Christ; not of those guilty of graver crimes who died unrepentant; and lastly of those whom the punishment sent by God had brought back to a saner mind, such as those whom the flood waters swept away. It is likely that many who had mocked Noah building the ark out of unbelief, as the waters slowly rose and brought common destruction, thought of God's justice and tried to appease it by sincere repentance, and took their very perishing as a ransom for their sins, offered in good heart to God: as we see even the worst criminals on the gallows bear torment with all patience and offer it to God, praying for mercy; and there is the thief's example, whom Christ so readily pardoned on the cross, because even at the end of his crimes he had confessed both Christ's majesty and his innocence. Grotius explains it of believers, and of those to whom faith in Christ had been preached but who were already dead, 'according to man': in the flesh, in men's reckoning, or by the guile and scheming of those who can kill only flesh and body; but they would live in spirit according to God, with the life of which God is author, the life of soul and spirit, as Stephen and James, who, taken from men, lived to God.

text: (e) Οἱ κατὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ τάξιν. Quod sic Maximus ad episcopos restringit, usum respicit suæ Ecclesiæ, quosimplicibus sacerdotibus indulgentur conjugia: sic nempe ille modeste, et ne videretur in cœlum os ponere, ac simplex monachus, sacerdotibus præscribere. Cæterum ejus ratio ad omnes Christi sacerdotio fungentes spectat; sunt enim illi omnes Melchisedeciani ordinis, non Aaronici, offerentes et ipsi panem et vinum (corpus scilicet ac sanguinem Christi conficientes) ac quos, perinde ac episcopos, maxima inde sanctitas ac castimonia deceat: quam et statuto suo ab eis Ecclesia sancte exigat, non ut templum Domini majoribus impudicitiis in se polluant, vere majestatis rei, quam sic adeant, quidquam indulgeat.
anchorLine: κατὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ τάξιν (e) ἱερατεύοντες ἐπίσκοποι
en: In limiting this to bishops Maximus has regard to the practice of his own Church, in which simple priests are allowed marriage; so he speaks modestly, so as not to seem to set his mouth against heaven and, as a mere monk, to lay down the law to priests. But his reasoning applies to all who serve in Christ's priesthood: they are all of the order of Melchizedek, not of Aaron, offering bread and wine themselves (making the body and blood of Christ), and, like bishops, the greatest holiness and chastity befit them. The Church by its rule rightly requires it of them, lest they defile the Lord's temple with the worst impurities and become guilty of offence against majesty, since no one should indulge a man who approaches it so.

text: (f) Τοὺς ἄρτους καὶ τὰ ποτήρια ἀνίσους. Triplicis προσφορᾶς (nos oblatas dicimus) meminit Liturgia Chrysostomi, sed velut quasi ex uno pane, cujus pars in Dei honorem et Christi immolationis memoriam offeratur; altera, in sanctæ Dei Genitricis; tertia, in omnium sanctorum memoriam, secundum distributionem novem ordinum angelorum, quibus accenseantur pro meritorum ratione etiam sancti. Maximus vero loqui videtur de panibus et calicibus, qui plures, pro sumentium Eucharistiam numerositate, vel pauciores offerrentur: impari tamen numero; quod vix alii observasse videntur. Sic memini legisse qui collectas in missa, sic impari numero recitandas statuant; sicque ternas diebus non solemnibus præscribunt rubricæ, cum alias addere occurrentis festi, seu justæ alicujus necessitatis, pietas non suaserit.
anchorLine: ποτήρια ἀνίσους (f) προτιθεῖν ἔθος τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ;
en: The Liturgy of Chrysostom mentions a threefold offering (we say oblations), but as if from one loaf, of which one part is offered in honour of God and in memory of Christ's sacrifice, a second for the holy Mother of God, and a third in memory of all the saints, by the arrangement of the nine orders of angels, with whom the saints too are counted according to merit. Maximus seems to speak of loaves and cups offered in greater or smaller number according to the number of communicants, yet in an uneven number, which hardly anyone else seems to have observed. So I remember reading that those who decree the collects at mass are to be recited in an odd number; and so the rubrics prescribe three on non-solemn days, unless piety urges adding others for a feast occurring or some just need.

anchorLine: Γαριζὶν (g) ἑρμηνεύεται περιτομή· Βὰλ δὲ, φύ-
en: The derivation of Garizin is well known, from the Hebrew root meaning 'to cut off, cut down'; so in the explanation of Bible names it is rendered 'axes' or 'cutters'. What follows, Maximus has 'Bal'; the rest have 'Gaibal', and the Hebrew itself is 'Ebal', explained as 'heap of age' or 'flowing heap': a heap is a mound; 'to mingle, pour over, mix' is the other root, to which Maximus's 'mass' looks; and the verb for 'to wear out' means to grow old, to be worn by age.
